newsitem.title: SWEDEN: OECD says unemployment, wages are Sweden's thorns.
newsitem.headline: OECD says unemployment, wages are Sweden's thorns.

text.p: Unemployment and labour policies are the thorns in Sweden's side with the country otherwise well-placed to take advantage of an upturn in world trade, the OECD said in a 1996/97 economic survey of Sweden.

The Organisation of Economic Cooperation and Development said Sweden has come a long way towards securing a more stable economic environment since 1994 with macroeconomic policies improving public finances, and both monetary policy credibility and exports strengthening economic activity in mid-1996.
But the OECD warned that Sweden's unemployment, currently running at above 12 percent including people on government schemes, and wages increases could hinder future growth.

"Laying the foundation for balanced growth and increased employment over the medium and long term .. is equally dependent on the progress to be made in improving labour market structures and raising the potential for growth in the market-based sectors of the economy," the OECD report said.

"In this respect pressing structural problems remain with respect to unemployment particularly in the area of wage formation but also with respect to the failure of small and medium sized firms in Sweden to expand."
The OECD said Sweden's labour market performance has deteriorated signficantly during the 1990s and improving job generating capacity was viewed as a key priority.

The OECD said a recent programme set out in the 1996 Employment Bill needs to be carried out without delay and extended to cover all dimensions of labour and product market flexibility, drawing in aspects of the OECD Jobs Strategy.

"Assisted by initiatives to produce markets with a greater role in the allocation of resources, and underpinned by ongoing fiscal consolidation, such a programme would allow for a more auspicious climate for overall economic development," the OECD said.

Most immediately reforms were needed to tax and transfer systems, employment security and industrial relations legislation, active labour market policies, education and training and competition-enhancing regulatory reform.
The OECD also sounded a warning note over wages. Sweden's nominal wages are currently increasing significantly faster than the average European rate in spite of high unemployment.
High unemployment failed to restrain wage settlements in the 1995 bargaining round, with awards in the more buoyant export industries such as paper and plup copied elsewhere.
"Given the commitment to price stability (with the inflation goal of two percent), high wage increases in upcoming wage rounds would be a major impediment to employment growth," the OECD said.

"Major changes in wages formation are required to achieve lower unemployment and the government's invitation to the social partners to present a joint proposal on how the wage formation process should be changed is an important move in this direction."
The OECD said the export-led Swedish recovery had prepared the economy to respond to a more vigorous expansion of exports.
Economic growth was forecast to rise from 1.75 percent in 1996 to over two percent in 1997 and 1998.
"Growth will be sustained by exports and business fixed investment .. the main doward risk to projections stems from the effect of the wages increases agreed for 1996/97," it said.
